references.text: Laban's accusation of stealing his daughters in v. 26 is met with his claim of ownership over them in v. 43, revealing his selfish view of the family.
Jacob's question 'What is my crime?' in v. 36 is the direct theological and rhetorical response to Laban's accusation that Jacob has deceived him in v. 26.
The motif of being robbed of one's children links Laban's false accusation against Jacob with Jacob's genuine grief over the loss of Joseph and Simeon, underscoring the theme of fatherhood and loss.
The identical phrasing 'What have you done?' creates an ironic mirror in which Jacob, who was previously deceived by Laban, is now accused of being the deceiver.
Both verses illustrate how innocent actions can be misinterpreted as great sins or crimes in a conflict between two parties.

The parallel between Laban's accusation that Jacob has caused trouble (v. 26) and Jacob's own complaint that his sons have caused trouble (Gen 34:30) highlights the theme of family warfare and its consequences.
